description: When the channels are purified: slimness of body and radiance; holding the breath at will, kindled digestive fire, the inner sound manifest, health.
Signs of success in haṭha: slim body, bright face, distinct inner sound, very clear eyes, freedom from disease, control of bindu, kindled fire, purified channels.
In the lowest (grade of breath-control) sweat, in the middle trembling, in the highest the breath reaches its place.
In mahāmudrā kuṇḍalinī straightens suddenly like a snake struck with a stick, and 'the state of death' arises (HYP 3.12).
Apāna rises to the fire, the flame grows, heats prāṇa; the body's fire blazes; kuṇḍalinī, heated, wakes like a struck serpent, hisses, straightens and enters the channel of Brahman as if into a hole.
From holding bindu a pleasant fragrance arises in the yogin's body.
Claims for khecarī (restricted practice): no disease, death, sleep, hunger, thirst or swooning; not bound by karma nor afflicted by time; bindu does not fall; poison has no effect.
Beginning stage: the knot of Brahmā pierced, bliss from the void, tinkling sounds (unstruck) within; the body divine, radiant, fragrant, healthy, heart full.
Ghaṭa stage: the united breath enters the middle, posture firm; the knot of Viṣṇu pierced, the sound of a kettledrum in the extreme void, indicating supreme bliss.
Paricaya stage: the sound of a drum (mardala); the breath in the great void, abode of all powers; natural bliss beyond the bliss of mind; no pain, age, disease, hunger or sleep.
Niṣpatti: the knot of Rudra pierced, the breath at Śiva's seat; sounds of flute and vīṇā; the mind becomes one — rājayoga.
At first ocean, thunder, kettledrum and cymbal sounds; in the middle drum, conch, bell and horn; at the end tinkling bells, flute, vīṇā and bee; the sounds become subtler as practice grows.
When mind and breath dissolve an indescribable bliss arises; breathing ceases, objects are not grasped, the yogin is motionless and changeless; the laya is known only to oneself, beyond speech.

In samādhi the body is like a log and hears no conch or drum; no smell, taste, form, touch or sound, no self or other; the mind neither asleep nor awake, free of memory and forgetting; no cold or heat, pleasure or pain, honour or dishonour; in waking as if asleep, without breath.
From the lowest breath-control sweat, from the middle trembling of the spine, from the highest leaving the ground.
From breath-control: moving in the sky, removal of disease, awakening of śakti, manonmanī, bliss in the mind.
In subtle meditation the awakened kuṇḍalinī goes out with the self through the eyes and roams the royal road, unseen because of her fickleness.
In devotional samādhi tears of bliss and thrilling of the hair arise, then a state beyond states, samādhi and manonmanī.
In the beginning stage the body becomes harmonious, fragrant, lustrous, the voice perfected; strong digestion, happiness, beauty, fullness of heart, strength.
Sweat, then trembling, then hopping like a frog, then leaving the ground in padmāsana; little sleep and excreta; no sweat, saliva or worms; freedom from disease.
In paricaya the breath stays in the space of suṣumnā, pierces the centres, and the yogin sees the 'three peaks' of his karma.
After gazing at one's shadow in bright sun, one's own image is seen in the sky; seeing it whole is a sign of long life and victory.
When the channels are purified: lightness of body, radiance, increase of the digestive fire, slimness.
Sweat, trembling, frog-like hopping, levitation in padmāsana; indifference to amount of food; little sleep and excreta; no worms, discharges, sweat or odour; great strength; a beautiful form.
Distant hearing and sight, instant travel, perfection of speech, taking forms at will, invisibility, turning iron to gold, moving in the sky — to be regarded as obstacles.
Women, captivated by the yogin's new beauty, seek union with him; yielding destroys bindu, shortens life and brings weakness.
In the mindless state the body is still as a log, sense-objects are not grasped, the breath stops, the mind neither sleeps nor wakes.
